references.authors: Uribarri J, Woodruff S, Goodman S, et al.
references.title: Advanced glycation end products in foods and a practical guide to their reduction in the diet.
references.finding: ELISA (CML immunoreactivity) database of 549 foods: dry heat raised AGEs 10- to 100-fold over the uncooked state; moist heat, shorter times, lower temperatures and lemon/vinegar marinades (which halved AGE formation in beef) reduced them; fat- and protein-rich animal foods ranked highest.

references.authors: Scheijen JLJM, Clevers E, Engelen L, et al.
references.title: Analysis of advanced glycation endproducts in selected food items by ultra-performance liquid chromatography tandem mass spectrometry: Presentation of a dietary AGE database.
references.finding: UPLC-MS/MS measurement of protein-bound CML, CEL and MG-H1 in 190 foods: highest levels in high-heat-processed nut and grain products and canned meats; fruits, vegetables, butter and coffee lowest.

references.authors: Kataoka H
references.title: Current Developments in Analytical Methods for Advanced Glycation End Products in Foods.
references.finding: Review of AGE analysis in foods that tabulates mass-spectrometry contents by food group, including Scheijen 2016 category ranges (e.g. bread MG-H1 13.5-231 mg/kg; savory spreads 204-445 mg/kg; cooked meats CML 0.8-48.2 mg/kg).

references.authors: Koschinsky T, He CJ, Mitsuhashi T, et al.
references.title: Orally absorbed reactive glycation products (glycotoxins): an environmental risk factor in diabetic nephropathy.
references.journal: Proc Natl Acad Sci U S A
references.n: 38 people with diabetes and 5 healthy controls
references.finding: After a single egg-white meal cooked with fructose, serum AGEs rose in proportion to the amount eaten; about 10% of ingested AGE (ELISA) appeared in serum and only about 30% of that was excreted in urine, less with kidney disease.

references.authors: Delgado-Andrade C, Tessier FJ, Niquet-Leridon C, et al.
references.title: Study of the urinary and faecal excretion of Nε-carboxymethyllysine in young human volunteers.
references.finding: A Maillard-rich diet doubled CML intake (11.3 vs 5.4 mg/day) and tripled faecal CML (3.5 vs 1.2 mg/day) while urinary CML did not rise in proportion, showing most dietary CML is not absorbed.

references.authors: Förster A, Kühne Y, Henle T
references.title: Studies on absorption and elimination of dietary maillard reaction products.
references.finding: About 50% of ingested free pyrraline and 60% of free pentosidine (from coffee) appeared in urine, but only 2% of peptide-bound pentosidine from pretzels; absorption differs widely between individual Maillard products.

references.authors: Scheijen JLJM, Hanssen NMJ, van Greevenbroek MM, et al.
references.title: Dietary intake of advanced glycation endproducts is associated with higher levels of advanced glycation endproducts in plasma and urine: The CODAM study.
references.finding: Higher FFQ-estimated intake of CML, CEL and MG-H1 (LC-MS/MS database) was associated with higher free plasma and urinary levels of the same AGEs (standardised beta about 0.18-0.25), but not with protein-bound plasma AGEs.

references.authors: Baye E, Kiriakova V, Uribarri J, et al.
references.title: Consumption of diets with low advanced glycation end products improves cardiometabolic parameters: meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials.
references.finding: Low-AGE diets lowered HOMA-IR (MD -1.3), total and LDL cholesterol, and individual trials reported lower 8-isoprostane, TNF-alpha and circulating AGEs; no change in weight, glucose, HbA1c or blood pressure.

references.authors: Clarke RE, Dordevic AL, Tan SM, et al.
references.title: Dietary Advanced Glycation End Products and Risk Factors for Chronic Disease: A Systematic Review of Randomised Controlled Trials.
references.finding: High-AGE diets raised circulating TNF-alpha and AGEs and raised 8-isoprostanes in healthy adults, but the authors called for higher-quality trials.

references.authors: Sohouli MH, Fatahi S, Sharifi-Zahabi E, et al.
references.title: The Impact of Low Advanced Glycation End Products Diet on Metabolic Risk Factors: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Randomized Controlled Trials.
references.finding: Low-AGE diets reduced HOMA-IR (WMD -1.2), fasting insulin, total and LDL cholesterol versus high-AGE diets, with no change in other metabolic-syndrome components.

references.authors: Lu X, Ma R, Zhan J, et al.
references.title: Effect of dietary intake of advanced glycation end products on biomarkers of type 2 diabetes: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
references.finding: High-AGE diets raised fasting glucose, insulin and HOMA-IR (SMD about 1.0-1.5) in pooled trials, especially in healthy participants.

references.authors: Kellow NJ, Savige GS
references.title: Dietary advanced glycation end-product restriction for the attenuation of insulin resistance, oxidative stress and endothelial dysfunction: a systematic review.
references.finding: Two 16-week trials in healthy adults favoured AGE restriction for 8-isoprostanes (SMD 0.9) and TNF-alpha, but 75% of trials lasted under 6 weeks and evidence quality was low to very low.

references.authors: Poulsen MW, Hedegaard RV, Andersen JM, et al.
references.title: Advanced glycation endproducts in food and their effects on health.
references.finding: Neither ELISA nor LC-MS covers all AGEs; most research relies on CML as a marker, only low-molecular-weight AGEs are absorbed, and the pro-inflammatory effects attributed to dietary AGEs come largely from feeding heated foods and need confirmation.

references.authors: Hellwig M, Diel P, Eisenbrand G, et al.
references.title: Dietary glycation compounds - implications for human health.
references.finding: German Research Foundation food-safety commission (SKLM) systematic assessment: human studies were small, short and confounded, animal effects needed doses far above human exposure, and there is at present no convincing evidence of a causal link between dietary glycation compounds and adverse health effects.

references.authors: Aglago EK, Mayén AL, Knaze V, et al.
references.title: Dietary Advanced Glycation End-Products and Colorectal Cancer Risk in the European Prospective Investigation into Cancer and Nutrition (EPIC) Study.
references.finding: Highest vs lowest quintile of LC-MS-estimated CML (HR 0.92) and MG-H1 (HR 0.92) intake was associated with slightly LOWER colorectal cancer risk; CEL showed no association. Cereals were the main CML/MG-H1 source.

references.authors: Pascual-Morena C, Garrido-Miguel M, Martínez-García I, et al.
references.title: Association of Dietary Advanced Glycation End Products with Overall and Site-Specific Cancer Risk and Mortality: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
references.finding: High dietary AGE intake was not associated with overall cancer risk (HR 0.99) but was associated with invasive breast cancer (HR 1.14) in a subset.

references.authors: Sharifi-Zahabi E, Soltani S, Hajizadeh-Sharafabad F, et al.
references.title: Dietary advanced glycation end-products (dAGEs) are not associated with the risk of cancer incidence. A systematic review and meta-analysis of prospective cohort studies.
references.finding: Dietary AGEs were not associated with cancer incidence (HR 1.04, 0.94-1.15).

references.authors: Ahmadirad H, Farhadnejad H, Norouzzadeh M, et al.
references.title: Uncovering the possible link between dietary advanced glycation end products and mortality risk: A systematic review and meta-analysis.
references.finding: Dietary AGE intake was not associated with all-cause (HR 1.02), cancer (HR 1.00) or cardiovascular (HR 1.16, NS) mortality.

references.authors: Linkens AM, Houben AJ, Niessen PM, et al.
references.title: A 4-week high-AGE diet does not impair glucose metabolism and vascular function in obese individuals.
references.finding: Double-blind 4-week diets differing 2.7-, 5.3- and 3.7-fold in CML, CEL and MG-H1 changed urinary and plasma AGEs but not insulin sensitivity (clamp), micro- or macrovascular function, inflammation or lipids.

references.authors: Linkens AMA, Houben AJHM, Kroon AA, et al.
references.title: Habitual intake of dietary advanced glycation end products is not associated with generalized microvascular function-the Maastricht Study.
references.finding: Habitual LC-MS-estimated AGE intake was not associated with retinal, skin or plasma markers of microvascular function or albuminuria.

references.authors: Linkens AMA, Eussen SJMP, Houben AJHM, et al.
references.title: Habitual intake of advanced glycation endproducts is not associated with worse insulin sensitivity, worse beta cell function, or presence of prediabetes or type 2 diabetes: The Maastricht Study.
references.finding: Habitual dietary AGE intake was not associated with worse insulin sensitivity, beta-cell function, prediabetes or type 2 diabetes.

references.authors: Semba RD, Gebauer SK, Baer DJ, et al.
references.title: Dietary intake of advanced glycation end products did not affect endothelial function and inflammation in healthy adults in a randomized controlled trial.
references.finding: Six weeks of isocaloric diets cooked at high versus mild temperatures changed serum and urine CML in the low-AGE arm but had no effect on endothelial function or inflammatory markers.

references.authors: de Courten B, de Courten MP, Soldatos G, et al.
references.title: Diet low in advanced glycation end products increases insulin sensitivity in healthy overweight individuals: a double-blind, randomized, crossover trial.
references.finding: Two weeks of a low-AGE diet (mass-spectrometry verified) raised clamp-measured insulin sensitivity by 1.3 mg/kg/min, an overall 2.1 mg/kg/min difference from the high-AGE diet.

references.authors: Mark AB, Poulsen MW, Andersen S, et al.
references.title: Consumption of a diet low in advanced glycation end products for 4 weeks improves insulin sensitivity in overweight women.
references.finding: Four weeks of low-AGE cooking lowered urinary AGEs (LC-MS/MS), fasting insulin and HOMA-IR versus a high-AGE diet after adjustment for anthropometric change.

references.authors: Uribarri J, Cai W, Peppa M, et al.
references.title: Circulating glycotoxins and dietary advanced glycation endproducts: two links to inflammatory response, oxidative stress, and aging.
references.journal: J Gerontol A Biol Sci Med Sci
references.finding: Dietary AGE intake (ELISA database) correlated with serum CML (r = 0.42) and CRP, and serum CML correlated with plasma 8-isoprostanes (r = 0.45), independent of age and calories.

references.authors: Vlassara H, Cai W, Goodman S, et al.
references.title: Protection against loss of innate defenses in adulthood by low advanced glycation end products (AGE) intake: role of the antiinflammatory AGE receptor-1.
references.n: 325 healthy adults, 66 CKD-3 patients; 40 healthy adults randomised
references.finding: A 30-50% lower-AGE diet for 4 months lowered serum AGEs, oxidant stress markers, RAGE and TNF-alpha in healthy adults and CKD patients (Vlassara/Uribarri group).

references.authors: Vlassara H, Cai W, Tripp E, et al.
references.title: Oral AGE restriction ameliorates insulin resistance in obese individuals with the metabolic syndrome: a randomised controlled trial.
references.n: 138 obese adults with metabolic syndrome (100 analysed)
references.finding: A 1-year low-AGE diet improved insulin resistance and lowered AGEs, oxidative stress and inflammation versus a regular diet; only laboratory staff were blinded.

references.authors: Negrean M, Stirban A, Stratmann B, et al.
references.title: Effects of low- and high-advanced glycation endproduct meals on macro- and microvascular endothelial function and oxidative stress in patients with type 2 diabetes mellitus.
references.finding: A meal with 15,100 vs 2,750 kU AGE (same ingredients, different cooking) reduced flow-mediated dilation by 36% vs 21% and raised oxidative-stress and endothelial markers more.

references.authors: Charissou A, Ait-Ameur L, Birlouez-Aragon I
references.title: Evaluation of a gas chromatography/mass spectrometry method for the quantification of carboxymethyllysine in food samples.
references.finding: An isotope-dilution GC-MS method for CML agreed with ELISA in powdered but not liquid infant formulas, illustrating matrix-dependent ELISA error.

references.authors: Ames JM
references.title: Determination of N epsilon-(carboxymethyl)lysine in foods and related systems.
references.finding: Immunochemical and instrumental CML methods each have drawbacks, extraction and hydrolysis are harder in foods than in plasma, and labs use different procedures; methods urgently need comparison and validation.

references.authors: Kanner J, Lapidot T
references.title: The stomach as a bioreactor: dietary lipid peroxidation in the gastric fluid and the effects of plant-derived antioxidants.
references.finding: Simulated gastric fluid amplified metmyoglobin- and iron-catalysed lipid peroxidation; heated muscle incubated 2 h accumulated hydroperoxides 6-fold to 1200 uM, and catechin or red-wine polyphenols prevented it.

references.authors: Kanner J
references.title: Dietary advanced lipid oxidation endproducts are risk factors to human health.
references.finding: Argues that dietary advanced lipid oxidation end-products (MDA, carbonyls, oxysterols) are partly absorbed, excreted in urine and may drive inflammation, and that antioxidants eaten with the meal limit their formation in the stomach.

references.authors: Gorelik S, Ligumsky M, Kohen R, et al.
references.title: A novel function of red wine polyphenols in humans: prevention of absorption of cytotoxic lipid peroxidation products.
references.finding: Plasma MDA rose by 160 nM (from 50 nM) after 250 g of heated turkey cutlets; red wine with the meal cut the rise 75% and cutlets soaked in wine before heating prevented it entirely; urine MDA followed.

references.authors: Gorelik S, Ligumsky M, Kohen R, et al.
references.title: The stomach as a "bioreactor": when red meat meets red wine.
references.finding: In rats fed red turkey-meat cutlets, stomach hydroperoxides and MDA accumulated and plasma MDA rose 50%; red-wine concentrate in the meal prevented the rise.

references.authors: Kanner J, Gorelik S, Roman S, et al.
references.title: Protection by polyphenols of postprandial human plasma and low-density lipoprotein modification: the stomach as a bioreactor.
references.finding: Summarises human data that plasma MDA roughly triples after a red-meat cutlet meal, modifies LDL, and is reduced about 75% by red-wine polyphenols taken with the meal.

references.authors: Sirota R, Gorelik S, Harris R, et al.
references.title: Coffee polyphenols protect human plasma from postprandial carbonyl modifications.
references.finding: 200 mL roasted coffee drunk with 250 g red-meat cutlets inhibited postprandial plasma MDA by 80% at 2 h and 50% at 4 h; roasted-ground coffee polyphenols were 2-5-fold more effective than instant in the stomach model.

references.authors: Tirosh O, Shpaizer A, Kanner J
references.title: Lipid Peroxidation in a Stomach Medium Is Affected by Dietary Oils (Olive/Fish) and Antioxidants: The Mediterranean versus Western Diet.
references.finding: In a simulated stomach, olive oil cut red-meat MDA from 122 to 48 uM (via oleic acid), whereas tuna or omega-3 oils raised it from 96 to 514 uM; vitamin E paradoxically increased peroxidation with fish oil.

references.authors: Kanner J, Selhub J, Shpaizer A, et al.
references.title: Redox homeostasis in stomach medium by foods: The Postprandial Oxidative Stress Index (POSI) for balancing nutrition and human health.
references.finding: Proposed a Postprandial Oxidative Stress Index: in simulated gastric fluid, 100 g portions of more than 50 plant foods inhibited peroxidation of 200 g red meat in proportion to their polyphenol content (R2 = 0.75).

references.authors: Li Z, Henning SM, Zhang Y, et al.
references.title: Antioxidant-rich spice added to hamburger meat during cooking results in reduced meat, plasma, and urine malondialdehyde concentrations.
references.finding: Adding a polyphenol-rich spice blend to hamburger meat before cooking cut MDA in the meat by 71% (0.52 vs 1.79 umol/250 g), prevented the rise in plasma MDA and lowered urinary MDA by 49%.

references.authors: Urquiaga I, Ávila F, Echeverria G, et al.
references.title: A Chilean Berry Concentrate Protects against Postprandial Oxidative Stress and Increases Plasma Antioxidant Activity in Healthy Humans.
references.finding: A Chilean berry concentrate taken with (and added to) a 250 g ground-turkey burger lowered postprandial plasma MDA and protein carbonyls and raised plasma antioxidant capacity.

references.authors: Urquiaga I, Troncoso D, Mackenna MJ, et al.
references.title: The Consumption of Beef Burgers Prepared with Wine Grape Pomace Flour Improves Fasting Glucose, Plasma Antioxidant Levels, and Oxidative Damage Markers in Humans: A Controlled Trial.
references.finding: One burger a day made with 7% grape-pomace flour for a month lowered oxLDL, advanced oxidation protein products and HOMA-IR, but plasma MDA did not change (non-randomised sequential design).

references.authors: Staprãns I, Rapp JH, Pan XM, et al.
references.title: Oxidized lipids in the diet are a source of oxidized lipid in chylomicrons of human serum.
references.finding: Feeding highly oxidised corn oil raised conjugated dienes in postprandial chylomicrons 4.7-fold and made them more oxidisable, showing dietary oxidised lipids are absorbed into blood.

references.authors: Staprans I, Pan XM, Rapp JH, et al.
references.title: Oxidized cholesterol in the diet is a source of oxidized lipoproteins in human serum.
references.finding: A meal with 400 mg alpha-epoxy cholesterol appeared in chylomicrons and then in LDL and HDL for up to 72 h, transferred by CETP, making LDL more oxidisable.

references.authors: Linseisen J, Wolfram G
references.title: Absorption of cholesterol oxidation products from ordinary foodstuff in humans.
references.finding: A salami-and-Parmesan meal naturally rich in cholesterol oxidation products raised plasma 7alpha-, 7beta-hydroxycholesterol and 7-ketocholesterol, peaking 8 h after the meal.

references.authors: Otaegui-Arrazola A, Menéndez-Carreño M, Ansorena D, et al.
references.title: Oxysterols: A world to explore.
references.finding: Oxysterols form in foods through heating, oxygen and light, are absorbed at different rates, and cholesterol oxidation products are cytotoxic, pro-apoptotic and pro-inflammatory in experimental studies.

references.authors: Savage GP, Dutta PC, Rodriguez-Estrada MT
references.title: Cholesterol oxides: their occurrence and methods to prevent their generation in foods.
references.finding: Tabulates food cholesterol oxides: spray-dried egg yolk 55-113 mg/100 g; egg yolk, stored meat, butter, cheese, cream and heated tallow 10-150 ug/g dry weight; grated cheeses 6-32 ug/g; traditional ghee about 12% of cholesterol; fresh egg yolk and fresh meat only traces; fried and stored hamburger rose from 8.4 to 49.5 ug/g.

references.authors: Khan MI, Min JS, Lee SO, et al.
references.title: Cooking, storage, and reheating effect on the formation of cholesterol oxidation products in processed meat products.
references.finding: In sausages, ham, bacon and luncheon meat, cooking produced COPs up to 0.73% of cholesterol (microwaving and oven grilling highest), and refrigerated storage with reheating raised them further (up to 3.3%).

references.authors: Chudy S, Teichert J
references.title: Oxysterols in stored powders as potential health hazards.
references.finding: In milk, egg and milk-egg powders stored 24 months, oxysterols rose steadily (to 1.81% of cholesterol in milk powder); eggs, heated milk products and fried meat are the main dietary oxysterol sources.

references.authors: Esterbauer H
references.title: Cytotoxicity and genotoxicity of lipid-oxidation products.
references.finding: Lipid-oxidation products such as 4-HNE and MDA are cytotoxic and genotoxic in cells and modify LDL, but the oral toxicity of oxidised lipids is unexpectedly low and their pathological significance unclear.

references.authors: Surh J, Kwon H
references.title: Estimation of daily exposure to 4-hydroxy-2-alkenals in Korean foods containing n-3 and n-6 polyunsaturated fatty acids.
references.finding: Estimated dietary exposure to 4-hydroxy-2-alkenals of 4.3 ug/day, plus more than 11.8 ug/day from fried foods (about 0.3 ug/kg/day), which the authors judged unlikely to pose a significant risk given tissue background levels.

references.authors: Tsikas D
references.title: Assessment of lipid peroxidation by measuring malondialdehyde (MDA) and relatives in biological samples: Analytical and biological challenges.
references.finding: MDA, HNE and F2-isoprostanes are hard to measure reliably: TBARS-type MDA assays are prone to pre-analytical and analytical artefacts, so reported changes are rarely free of doubt.

references.authors: Halliwell B, Zhao K, Whiteman M
references.title: The gastrointestinal tract: a major site of antioxidant action?
references.finding: Diet supplies pro-oxidants (iron, heme, lipid peroxides, aldehydes, nitrite) and poorly absorbed polyphenols and carotenoids reach high concentrations in the gut lumen, making the GI tract a plausible main site of dietary antioxidant action.

references.authors: Williams MJ, Sutherland WH, McCormick MP, et al.
references.title: Normal endothelial function after meals rich in olive or safflower oil previously used for deep frying.
references.finding: Meals rich in olive or safflower oil used for 8 hours of deep-frying, with high peroxide and carbonyl content, raised triglycerides but did not change flow-mediated dilation.

references.authors: Perez-Herrera A, Rangel-Zuñiga OA, Delgado-Lista J, et al.
references.title: The antioxidants in oils heated at frying temperature, whether natural or added, could protect against postprandial oxidative stress in obese people.
references.finding: A breakfast made with sunflower oil heated through 20 frying cycles lowered plasma GSH, raised protein carbonyls and NADPH-oxidase gene expression more than the same breakfast made with heated virgin olive oil or antioxidant-enriched seed oil.

references.authors: Rangel-Zuñiga OA, Haro C, Tormos C, et al.
references.title: Frying oils with high natural or added antioxidants content, which protect against postprandial oxidative stress, also protect against DNA oxidation damage.
references.finding: Postprandial 8-OHdG was lower after breakfasts with repeatedly heated virgin olive oil or antioxidant-enriched oil than after heated sunflower oil, which activated p53-dependent DNA-repair genes.

references.authors: Rueda-Clausen CF, Silva FA, Lindarte MA, et al.
references.title: Olive, soybean and palm oils intake have a similar acute detrimental effect over the endothelial function in healthy young subjects.
references.finding: A potato-soup meal with 60 mL olive, soybean or palm oil, fresh or after 10 or 20 deep-fries, all reduced flow-mediated dilation similarly (about 32%) at 3 h.

references.authors: Higdon JV, Liu J, Du SH, et al.
references.title: Supplementation of postmenopausal women with fish oil rich in eicosapentaenoic acid and docosahexaenoic acid is not associated with greater in vivo lipid peroxidation compared with oils rich in oleate and linoleate as assessed by plasma malondialdehyde and F(2)-isoprostanes.
references.finding: Fish oil supplying 3.4 g/day EPA+DHA did not raise plasma F2-isoprostanes or MDA compared with oleate- or linoleate-rich oils (values were lower after fish oil), although TBARS rose.

references.authors: Mori TA, Dunstan DW, Burke V, et al.
references.title: Effect of dietary fish and exercise training on urinary F2-isoprostane excretion in non-insulin-dependent diabetic patients.
references.finding: Adding one fish meal a day (3.6 g omega-3/day) to a low-fat diet for 8 weeks lowered urinary F2-isoprostanes by 20%.

references.authors: Pierre F, Peiro G, Taché S, et al.
references.title: New marker of colon cancer risk associated with heme intake: 1,4-dihydroxynonane mercapturic acid.
references.n: human crossover arm plus rat studies
references.finding: Urinary DHN-MA (the main 4-HNE metabolite) tracked heme intake: in a randomised human crossover, adding heme iron to a 60 g/day red-meat diet doubled DHN-MA, whereas urinary 8-iso-PGF2alpha did not rise in humans.

references.authors: Pierre FH, Martin OC, Santarelli RL, et al.
references.title: Calcium and α-tocopherol suppress cured-meat promotion of chemically induced colon carcinogenesis in rats and reduce associated biomarkers in human volunteers.
references.n: human volunteers (crossover, 180 g/day cured meat for 4 days) plus rats
references.finding: Cured meat raised faecal N-nitroso compounds and lipoperoxidation markers in human stools; calcium carbonate normalised both and alpha-tocopherol added to the meat lowered faecal lipoperoxidation.

references.authors: Joosen AM, Kuhnle GG, Aspinall SM, et al.
references.title: Effect of processed and red meat on endogenous nitrosation and DNA damage.
references.finding: 420 g/day (men) or 366 g/day (women) of fresh red or nitrite-cured meat raised faecal N-nitroso compounds about 50-fold over a vegetarian diet (175-185 vs 2.6-3.5 nmol/g); cured meat raised oxidised pyrimidines in faecal-water-treated cells, though the vegetarian diet surprisingly caused more strand breaks.

references.authors: Bingham SA, Hughes R, Cross AJ
references.title: Effect of white versus red meat on endogenous N-nitrosation in the human colon and further evidence of a dose response.
references.finding: Faecal apparent total N-nitroso compounds rose linearly with red meat from 0 to 420 g/day (r = 0.97; about 2.6 ug/day per g meat), while 420-600 g/day of white meat had no effect.

references.authors: Bastide NM, Pierre FH, Corpet DE
references.title: Heme iron from meat and risk of colorectal cancer: a meta-analysis and a review of the mechanisms involved.
references.finding: Highest vs lowest heme intake: colon cancer RR 1.18 (1.06-1.32); rat studies consistently show heme and red meat promote precancerous lesions via N-nitrosation and lipid-peroxidation aldehydes.

references.authors: Qiao L, Feng Y
references.title: Intakes of heme iron and zinc and colorectal cancer incidence: a meta-analysis of prospective studies.
references.finding: Colorectal cancer RR 1.14 for highest vs lowest heme iron intake and 1.11 per 1 mg/day of heme.

references.authors: Fonseca-Nunes A, Jakszyn P, Agudo A
references.title: Iron and cancer risk--a systematic review and meta-analysis of the epidemiological evidence.
references.finding: Each 1 mg/day of heme iron was associated with colorectal (RR 1.08, 1.00-1.17) and colon cancer (RR 1.12); a tendency toward positive association with cancer overall.

references.authors: Cross AJ, Ferrucci LM, Risch A, et al.
references.title: A large prospective study of meat consumption and colorectal cancer risk: an investigation of potential mechanisms underlying this association.
references.finding: Red (HR 1.24) and processed meat (HR 1.16) were linked to colorectal cancer, with heme iron (HR 1.13), nitrate from processed meat (HR 1.16) and the HCAs MeIQx and DiMeIQx (HR 1.17-1.19) as candidate mechanisms.

references.authors: Cross AJ, Harnly JM, Ferrucci LM, et al.
references.title: Developing a heme iron database for meats according to meat type, cooking method and doneness level.
references.finding: Heme iron in cooked US meats: hamburger mean 10.3 ug/g, steak 9.3, pork products 3.4 (chop) to 7.5 (ham), chicken breast 2.4; cooking method and doneness made no consistent difference.

references.authors: Pretorius B, Schönfeldt HC, Hall N
references.title: Total and haem iron content lean meat cuts and the contribution to the diet.
references.finding: Raw lean beef, lamb, pork and chicken contained 1.58, 1.64, 0.81 and 0.78 mg total iron/100 g, of which 77%, 81%, 88% and 74% was heme.

references.authors: Valenzuela C, de Romaña DL, Olivares M, et al.
references.title: Total iron and heme iron content and their distribution in beef meat and viscera.
references.finding: Beef muscle cuts averaged 1.4 mg total iron/100 g with 64% as heme; liver had 6.0 mg/100 g but only 13.6% heme.

references.authors: Wheal MS, DeCourcy-Ireland E, Bogard JR, et al.
references.title: Measurement of haem and total iron in fish, shrimp and prawn using ICP-MS: Implications for dietary iron intake calculations.
references.finding: Total iron ranged 0.55-14.43 mg/100 g fresh weight and heme iron 18-93% of total across species; single acetone extractions underestimate heme.

references.authors: Hodgson JM, Ward NC, Burke V, et al.
references.title: Increased lean red meat intake does not elevate markers of oxidative stress and inflammation in humans.
references.finding: Replacing carbohydrate foods with about 200 g/day of lean red meat did not raise plasma F2-isoprostanes and lowered urinary F2-isoprostanes (-137 pmol/mmol creatinine) and white-cell counts versus usual diet.

references.authors: O'Connor LE, Kim JE, Clark CM, et al.
references.title: Effects of Total Red Meat Intake on Glycemic Control and Inflammatory Biomarkers: A Meta-Analysis of Randomized Controlled Trials.
references.finding: Diets with at least 0.5 servings/day of total red meat for up to 16 weeks did not change glucose, insulin, HOMA-IR, HbA1c or CRP compared with less red meat.

references.authors: Lescinsky H, Afshin A, Ashbaugh C, et al.
references.title: Health effects associated with consumption of unprocessed red meat: a Burden of Proof study.
references.finding: Burden of Proof analysis: weak evidence linking unprocessed red meat to colorectal cancer, breast cancer, type 2 diabetes and ischaemic heart disease, and no evidence for stroke; the risk-minimising intake had a 0-200 g/day uncertainty interval.

references.authors: Johnston BC, Zeraatkar D, Han MA, et al.
references.title: Unprocessed Red Meat and Processed Meat Consumption: Dietary Guideline Recommendations From the Nutritional Recommendations (NutriRECS) Consortium.
references.finding: NutriRECS panel (GRADE) suggested adults continue current unprocessed and processed meat consumption (weak recommendation, low-certainty evidence); the guideline drew multiple published letters of objection.

references.authors: Bao W, Rong Y, Rong S, et al.
references.title: Dietary iron intake, body iron stores, and the risk of type 2 diabetes: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
references.finding: Type 2 diabetes RR 1.33 for highest vs lowest heme iron intake and 1.16 per 1 mg/day; ferritin was also associated with diabetes.

references.authors: Bouvard V, Loomis D, Guyton KZ, et al.
references.title: Carcinogenicity of consumption of red and processed meat.
references.finding: IARC classified processed meat as carcinogenic to humans (Group 1) and red meat as probably carcinogenic (Group 2A), estimating colorectal cancer risk up about 18% per 50 g/day of processed meat and 17% per 100 g/day of red meat.

references.authors: EFSA Panel on Contaminants in the Food Chain (EFSA CONTAM Panel)
references.title: Risk assessment of N-nitrosamines in food.
references.finding: EFSA: margins of exposure to 10 carcinogenic N-nitrosamines in food at the 95th percentile were 48-3337 (well below 10,000) for all age groups, a health concern; meat and meat products were the main contributors.

references.authors: EFSA Panel on Food Additives and Nutrient Sources added to Food (ANS)
references.title: Re-evaluation of potassium nitrite (E 249) and sodium nitrite (E 250) as food additives.
references.finding: EFSA set an ADI of 0.07 mg nitrite/kg/day; exposure from additives was within it, but margins of exposure to preformed nitrosamines in meat products were below 10,000 at high intake, with epidemiological links of nitrite plus nitrate from processed meat to colorectal cancer.

references.authors: Eisenbrand G, Buettner A, Diel P, et al.
references.title: Commentary of the SKLM to the EFSA opinion on risk assessment of N-nitrosamines in food.
references.finding: SKLM commentary on EFSA's nitrosamine opinion: endogenous NDMA formation may exceed dietary exposure by about 2-3 orders of magnitude, so dietary-only margins of exposure give an incomplete risk picture.

references.authors: Loh YH, Jakszyn P, Luben RN, et al.
references.title: N-Nitroso compounds and cancer incidence: the European Prospective Investigation into Cancer and Nutrition (EPIC)-Norfolk Study.
references.finding: Dietary NDMA was associated with gastrointestinal (HR 1.13 per SD) and especially rectal cancer (HR 1.46 per SD); the endogenous N-nitroso index and dietary nitrite were not.

references.authors: Sinha R, Rothman N, Brown ED, et al.
references.title: High concentrations of the carcinogen 2-amino-1-methyl-6-phenylimidazo- [4,5-b]pyridine (PhIP) occur in chicken but are dependent on the cooking method.
references.finding: Pan-fried, oven-broiled and grilled chicken breast contained 12-480 ng/g PhIP, rising with doneness and browning; roasted or stewed whole chicken had none.

references.authors: Sinha R, Rothman N, Salmon CP, et al.
references.title: Heterocyclic amine content in beef cooked by different methods to varying degrees of doneness and gravy made from meat drippings.
references.finding: In beef, MeIQx rose with doneness to 8.2 ng/g and PhIP in steak ranged 1.9-30 ng/g; oven-roast beef contained no HCAs, but gravy from well-done roast drippings had 2 ng/g PhIP and 7 ng/g MeIQx.

references.authors: Sinha R, Knize MG, Salmon CP, et al.
references.title: Heterocyclic amine content of pork products cooked by different methods and to varying degrees of doneness.
references.finding: Very well done oven-broiled bacon had 30.3 ng/g PhIP; pan-fried very well done sausage patties 5.4 ng/g MeIQx; hot dogs and ham slices had low or undetectable HCAs.

references.authors: Kazerouni N, Sinha R, Hsu CH, et al.
references.title: Analysis of 200 food items for benzo[a]pyrene and estimation of its intake in an epidemiologic study.
references.finding: Benzo[a]pyrene reached about 4 ng/g in very well done grilled/barbecued steaks and hamburgers and well-done grilled chicken with skin, was lower in broiled or pan-fried meat, and bread/cereals (29%) and grilled meat (21%) supplied most intake.

references.authors: Duedahl-Olesen L, Ionas AC
references.title: Formation and mitigation of PAHs in barbecued meat - a review.
references.finding: PAHs in barbecued meat come from incomplete combustion, fat pyrolysis and fat-induced flames; removing char, limiting dripping, acidic marinades, spices and leaner cuts reduce benzo[a]pyrene.

references.authors: Viegas O, Yebra-Pimentel I, Martínez-Carballo E, et al.
references.title: Effect of beer marinades on formation of polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons in charcoal-grilled pork.
references.finding: Marinating pork in black beer before charcoal grilling cut the 8 EFSA marker PAHs by 53% (non-alcoholic Pilsner 25%, Pilsner 13%), in line with the marinades' radical-scavenging activity.

references.authors: Tareke E, Rydberg P, Karlsson P, et al.
references.title: Analysis of acrylamide, a carcinogen formed in heated foodstuffs.
references.finding: Acrylamide was 5-50 ug/kg in heated protein-rich foods and 150-4000 ug/kg in heated carbohydrate-rich foods such as potato products and crispbread; boiled or unheated foods had <5 ug/kg.

references.authors: Powers SJ, Mottram DS, Curtis A, et al.
references.title: Acrylamide levels in potato crisps in Europe from 2002 to 2016.
references.journal: Food Addit Contam Part A Chem Anal Control Expo Risk Assess
references.finding: Mean acrylamide in potato crisps fell 53% from 763 ng/g (2002) to 358 ng/g (2011) and was 412 ng/g in 2016, highest in the first half of the year when stored potatoes were used.

references.authors: Navruz-Varlı S, Mortaş H
references.title: Acrylamide formation in air-fried versus deep and oven-fried potatoes.
references.finding: Home-prepared potato sticks had low acrylamide whether air-fried (12.2 ug/kg), deep-fried (8.9) or oven-fried (7.4), with no significant difference by method; soaking reduced levels.

references.authors: Sansano M, Juan-Borrás M, Escriche I, et al.
references.title: Effect of pretreatments and air-frying, a novel technology, on acrylamide generation in fried potatoes.
references.finding: At 180 C, air-frying cut acrylamide in potatoes by about 90% compared with deep-oil frying; soaking pretreatments cut deep-fried acrylamide by up to 80-90%.

references.authors: Törős G, Alibrahem W, Kharrat Helu N, et al.
references.title: Acrylamide in Food: From Maillard Reaction to Public Health Concern.
references.finding: Review tabulating acrylamide ranges by food (e.g. crisps 21-3444, biscuits <20-2144, French fries <20-1068 ug/kg) and EU 2017/2158 benchmark levels (wheat bread 50, breakfast cereals 300, biscuits 350, fried potato 500, crisps 750, roast coffee 400, instant coffee 850 ug/kg).

references.authors: Smith JS, Ameri F, Gadgil P
references.title: Effect of marinades on the formation of heterocyclic amines in grilled beef steaks.
references.finding: One-hour commercial spice marinades cut total HCAs in grilled beef steak by 57-88% (Caribbean 88%, herb 72%, Southwest 57%), correlating with carnosic acid, carnosol and rosmarinic acid content.

references.authors: Salmon CP, Knize MG, Felton JS
references.title: Effects of marinating on heterocyclic amine carcinogen formation in grilled chicken.
references.finding: A sugar-oil-vinegar-garlic-mustard-lemon marinade cut PhIP in grilled chicken by 92-99% and total HCAs from 56 to 1.7, 158 to 10 and 330 to 44 ng/g at 20, 30 and 40 min, though MeIQx rose over 10-fold at the longest times.

references.authors: Felton JS, Fultz E, Dolbeare FA, et al.
references.title: Effect of microwave pretreatment on heterocyclic aromatic amine mutagens/carcinogens in fried beef patties.
references.finding: Microwaving beef patties 1-3 min before frying removed precursors and fat and cut the four main HCAs 3- to 9-fold and mutagenicity up to 95%.

references.authors: Martínez Góngora V, Matthes KL, Castaño PR, et al.
references.title: Dietary Heterocyclic Amine Intake and Colorectal Adenoma Risk: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis.
references.finding: Top vs bottom intake of PhIP (OR 1.20), MeIQx (OR 1.20), DiMeIQx (OR 1.16) and benzo[a]pyrene (OR 1.15) was associated with colorectal adenoma, with dose-response for PhIP and MeIQx.

references.authors: Ollberding NJ, Wilkens LR, Henderson BE, et al.
references.title: Meat consumption, heterocyclic amines and colorectal cancer risk: the Multiethnic Cohort Study.
references.finding: Neither red or processed meat nor estimated HCA intake was associated with colorectal cancer risk.

references.authors: Qin P, Zhang M, Han M, et al.
references.title: Fried-food consumption and risk of cardiovascular disease and all-cause mortality: a meta-analysis of observational studies.
references.finding: Highest vs lowest fried-food intake: major CVD RR 1.28, CHD 1.22, heart failure 1.37, but no association with cardiovascular (1.02) or all-cause mortality (1.03); heterogeneity was high.

references.authors: Guallar-Castillón P, Rodríguez-Artalejo F, Lopez-Garcia E, et al.
references.title: Consumption of fried foods and risk of coronary heart disease: Spanish cohort of the European Prospective Investigation into Cancer and Nutrition study.
references.finding: Fried-food intake was not associated with coronary heart disease (top quarter HR 1.08) or mortality, whether olive or sunflower oil was used.

references.authors: Bloomer RJ, Kabir MM, Marshall KE, et al.
references.title: Postprandial oxidative stress in response to dextrose and lipid meals of differing size.
references.finding: Only a 66 g fat load (heavy cream) raised plasma MDA and H2O2; 33 g fat and 75 or 150 g dextrose produced minimal oxidative stress.

references.authors: Fisher-Wellman KH, Bloomer RJ
references.title: Exacerbated postprandial oxidative stress induced by the acute intake of a lipid meal compared to isoenergetically administered carbohydrate, protein, and mixed meals in young, healthy men.
references.finding: Among isocaloric lipid, carbohydrate, protein and mixed meals, only the lipid meal raised H2O2, MDA and nitrate/nitrite over 2-6 h.

references.authors: Ceriello A, Quagliaro L, Piconi L, et al.
references.title: Effect of postprandial hypertriglyceridemia and hyperglycemia on circulating adhesion molecules and oxidative stress generation and the possible role of simvastatin treatment.
references.finding: A high-fat meal and 75 g glucose each raised nitrotyrosine and adhesion molecules, with additive effects when combined; simvastatin blunted the response.

references.authors: Bae JH, Bassenge E, Kim KB, et al.
references.title: Postprandial hypertriglyceridemia impairs endothelial function by enhanced oxidant stress.
references.finding: Two hours after a high-fat meal, triglycerides and leukocyte superoxide production rose and flow-mediated dilation fell from 13.7% to 8.2%; changes in superoxide correlated with FMD (r = -0.78); a low-fat meal had no effect.

references.authors: Plotnick GD, Corretti MC, Vogel RA
references.title: Effect of antioxidant vitamins on the transient impairment of endothelium-dependent brachial artery vasoactivity following a single high-fat meal.
references.finding: A 900 kcal, 50 g fat breakfast cut flow-mediated dilation from 20% to 8-12% for 2-4 h, while a fat-free 900 kcal meal did not; pretreatment with 1 g vitamin C and 800 IU vitamin E blocked the fall.

references.authors: Ghanim H, Sia CL, Upadhyay M, et al.
references.title: Orange juice neutralizes the proinflammatory effect of a high-fat, high-carbohydrate meal and prevents endotoxin increase and Toll-like receptor expression.
references.finding: A 900 kcal high-fat high-carbohydrate meal with water or glucose raised NADPH-oxidase p47phox, leukocyte ROS, endotoxin and Toll-like receptors; drinking 300 kcal orange juice with it prevented these rises.

references.authors: Burton-Freeman B, Linares A, Hyson D, et al.
references.title: Strawberry modulates LDL oxidation and postprandial lipemia in response to high-fat meal in overweight hyperlipidemic men and women.
references.finding: A strawberry beverage (10 g freeze-dried fruit) taken with a high-fat meal lowered postprandial triglycerides and oxidised LDL compared with placebo.

references.authors: Sies H, Stahl W, Sevanian A
references.title: Nutritional, dietary and postprandial oxidative stress.
references.finding: Postprandial oxidative stress follows sustained hyperlipidaemia and hyperglycaemia; dietary lipid hydroperoxides are absorbed, and antioxidants supplied with a meal rich in oxidised or oxidisable fat attenuate the response.

references.authors: Fewkes JJ, Kellow NJ, Cowan SF, et al.
references.title: A single, high-fat meal adversely affects postprandial endothelial function: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
references.finding: A single high-fat meal lowered flow-mediated dilation by about 1.0-1.2 percentage points at 2-4 h; the fall was larger in younger, leaner people, and meal fat percentage was inversely associated with the 3-h change.

references.authors: Vogel RA, Corretti MC, Plotnick GD
references.title: The postprandial effect of components of the Mediterranean diet on endothelial function.
references.finding: Five 900 kcal, 50 g fat meals all raised triglycerides; the olive-oil meal cut FMD 31%, but olive oil with balsamic vinegar and salad, or with vitamins C and E, and salmon or canola-oil meals did not significantly reduce FMD.

references.authors: Mohanty P, Hamouda W, Garg R, et al.
references.title: Glucose challenge stimulates reactive oxygen species (ROS) generation by leucocytes.
references.finding: 75 g glucose raised leukocyte ROS generation to about 240% of baseline at 2 h, increased p47phox and lowered alpha-tocopherol.

references.authors: Meagher EA, Barry OP, Burke A, et al.
references.title: Alcohol-induced generation of lipid peroxidation products in humans.
references.finding: Acute alcohol raised urinary isoprostanes in a time- and dose-dependent way tracking blood alcohol (placebo-controlled, double-blind); isoprostanes were markedly elevated in alcoholic liver disease.

references.authors: Schrieks IC, van den Berg R, Sierksma A, et al.
references.title: Effect of red wine consumption on biomarkers of oxidative stress.
references.finding: Four weeks of 450 mL/day red wine (41 g alcohol) raised urinary 8-iso-PGF2alpha versus dealcoholised red wine (157 vs 141 pg/mg creatinine).

references.authors: Wood AM, Kaptoge S, Butterworth AS, et al.
references.title: Risk thresholds for alcohol consumption: combined analysis of individual-participant data for 599 912 current drinkers in 83 prospective studies.
references.finding: All-cause mortality was lowest at about 100 g alcohol/week or less and rose above that threshold.

references.authors: Zhao J, Stockwell T, Naimi T, et al.
references.title: Association Between Daily Alcohol Intake and Risk of All-Cause Mortality: A Systematic Review and Meta-analyses.
references.finding: After adjusting for former-drinker and other biases, low-volume drinking was not associated with lower all-cause mortality, and risk rose at higher intakes.

references.authors: Jomova K, Valko M
references.title: Advances in metal-induced oxidative stress and human disease.
references.finding: Redox-active metals (iron, copper, chromium) generate ROS by Fenton chemistry, whereas cadmium, lead and arsenic act mainly by binding thiols and depleting glutathione.

references.authors: Mozaffarian D, Rimm EB
references.title: Fish intake, contaminants, and human health: evaluating the risks and the benefits.
references.finding: Modest fish intake (1-2 servings/week) cut coronary death 36% and total mortality 17%; apart from a few high-mercury species, benefits outweigh methylmercury risks for adults.

references.authors: EFSA Panel on Contaminants in the Food Chain (CONTAM)
references.title: Update of the risk assessment of inorganic arsenic in food.
references.finding: EFSA set a BMDL05 of 0.06 ug/kg/day for inorganic arsenic (skin cancer); adult margins of exposure of 0.4-2 (mean) raise a health concern.

references.authors: Snoj Tratnik J, Kocman D, Horvat M, et al.
references.title: Cadmium exposure in adults across Europe: Results from the HBM4EU Aligned Studies survey 2014-2020.
references.finding: Urinary cadmium exceeded age-dependent alert values in 16% of participants (1.4-42% across study sites).
